slides.title: Theoretical Microeconomics

slides.html:
What you will be able to do

  1. Solve a consumer's or firm's problem by hand (best bundle, cheapest production, response to prices)
  2. Find market-clearing prices in a small economy and check efficiency
  3. Solve a small game: dominance, Nash (pure and mixed), backward induction
  4. Explain with numbers why hidden information distorts contracts
  5. Design a simple rule: an auction with a reserve, a menu of contracts

Small numbers, every step shown. Proofs can be skipped; each has a one-sentence summary in the notes.
slides.title: What you will be able to do

slides.html:
One Thread: Optimisation, Equilibrium, Efficiency

  1. Individual optimisation: given constraints, what does a rational agent choose?
  2. Equilibrium: everyone optimises at once — what is stable?
  3. Efficiency and design: is it good? Can the rules change?

Toolbox: maximum theorem · Lagrange/KT · envelope theorem · duality · separating hyperplane · Brouwer/Kakutani · backward induction · revelation principle
slides.title: One Thread: Optimisation, Equilibrium, Efficiency

slides.html:
Roadmap

Ch. Topic Core question

3 Uncertainty How to choose under risk?

slides.title: Roadmap

slides.html:
1. Preferences and Utility

Utility is just notation for a ranking
slides.title: 1. Preferences and Utility

slides.html:
Axioms of Preference

Axiom Meaning
Complete, transitive rational: comparable, no cycles (else a "money pump")
Continuous no jumps
Strictly monotone more is better
(Strict) convexity likes balanced bundles
Homothetic doubling income scales choices

Complete + transitive + continuous + strictly monotone ⟹ a continuous utility exists (construct along the diagonal x\sim U(x)e).
slides.title: Axioms of Preference

slides.html:
Worked example: a money pump

Preferences: apple \succ banana \succ cherry \succ apple (a cycle). Pay 1 for each swap to a preferred fruit:

banana \to apple \to cherry \to banana: back at the start, 3 poorer.

Transitivity rules out cycles. Without continuity a ranking (lexicographic order) may have no utility function.
slides.title: Worked example: a money pump

slides.html:
Properties of Utility

  • Ordinal: V=g(U) (g strictly increasing) represents the same preferences
  • U strictly increasing ⟺ monotone; quasi-concave ⟺ convex preferences
  • Homothetic ⟺ utility can be taken homogeneous of degree one
  • MRS_{ij}=U_i/U_j; \sigma_{ij}=\dfrac{d\ln(x_i/x_j)}{d\ln(U_j/U_i)}
  • CES: \sigma=1/(1-\rho); \rho\to0 is Cobb–Douglas
slides.title: Properties of Utility

slides.html:
Worked example: Alice's tastes

U=\sqrt{x_1x_2}: (4,1), (2,2), (1,4) all give U=2; (3,3) gives 3.

  • V=U^2=x_1x_2: same ranking (ordinality); W=x_1+x_2: different ranking
  • MRS=x_2/x_1: \tfrac14 at (4,1), 1 at (2,2), 4 at (1,4) — falling as she gets more of good 1
slides.title: Worked example: Alice's tastes

slides.html:
2. Consumer Theory

Two mirror-image problems: fix the budget, or fix the utility
slides.title: 2. Consumer Theory

slides.html:
Solution and Indirect Utility

  • Unique solution, budget exhausted
  • KT: \dfrac{U_i}{U_j}=\dfrac{p_i}{p_j}; \lambda = shadow price
  • Cobb–Douglas: x_1^*=\dfrac{aI}{p_1}, fixed budget shares

V(p,I): continuous, degree-0 homogeneous, increasing in I, decreasing in p, quasi-convex

Roy's identity

x_i=-\frac{\partial V/\partial p_i}{\partial V/\partial I}
slides.title: Solution and Indirect Utility

slides.html:
Worked example: Alice's budget

U=x_1^{0.4}x_2^{0.6}, I=100, p=(2,5):

x_1^*=\tfrac{0.4\cdot100}2=20,\quad x_2^*=\tfrac{0.6\cdot100}5=12
  • budget: 40+60=100 ✓
  • MRS=\tfrac{0.4\cdot12}{0.6\cdot20}=0.4=\tfrac25=p_1/p_2 ✓
  • U\approx14.72, \lambda=U_1/p_1\approx0.147
  • perfect complements: x_1=x_2=100/7; perfect substitutes: spend all on the cheaper good
slides.title: Worked example: Alice's budget

slides.html:
Expenditure Minimisation (EMP)

e(p,U)=\min_x p\cdot x\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ U(x)\ge U_0
  • Increasing in p, degree-one homogeneous, concave
  • Shephard's lemma: \partial e/\partial p_i=x_i^H (Hicksian demand)
  • Concavity: consumers can re-optimise, so expenditure grows slower than linearly
slides.title: Expenditure Minimisation (EMP)

slides.html:
Worked example: Roy and Shephard in numbers

V=0.5102\,I/(p_1^{0.4}p_2^{0.6})\approx14.72 at (p,I)=((2,5),100).

  • \partial V/\partial I=0.1472, \partial V/\partial p_1=-2.944 ⟹ Roy: x_1=2.944/0.1472=20
  • e(p,14.72)\approx100 = her income (duality)
  • Shephard: \partial e/\partial p_1=0.4\cdot100/2=20
slides.title: Worked example: Roy and Shephard in numbers

slides.html:
Worked example: a price rise in numbers

p_1:\ 2\to2.5 (Alice, U=14.72):

Step x_1 Change
start 20
compensated (Hicks) at new price 17.49 substitution -2.51
final (Marshall) 16 income -1.49

Total -4=-2.51-1.49. Compensation needed: 100\cdot1.25^{0.4}-100=9.34.
slides.title: Worked example: a price rise in numbers

slides.html:
The Slutsky Matrix

  • S=[\partial x_i^H/\partial p_j]=\nabla^2_pe: symmetric, negative semi-definite, Sp=0
  • Compensated demand slopes down; cross substitution effects are symmetric
  • Giffen good: inferior and the income effect beats substitution
slides.title: The Slutsky Matrix

slides.html:
Integrability and Revealed Preference

Integrability: budget balance + symmetric NSD Slutsky matrix ⟺ demand comes from quasi-concave utility.

u(x)=\max\{u:\,p\cdot x\ge e(p,u)\ \forall p\}

WARP: p^1x^1\ge p^1x^2\Rightarrow p^2x^1>p^2x^2

WARP + budget balance ⟹ homogeneous of degree 0, NSD Slutsky
slides.title: Integrability and Revealed Preference

slides.html:
Worked example: testing WARP on data

Obs. Prices Choice Cost
1 (1,2) (4,2) 8
2 (1,3) (2,3) 11
  • at p^1, x^2 costs 8 \le8 ⟹ x^1 revealed preferred to x^2
  • at p^2, x^1 costs 10\le11 ⟹ x^2 revealed preferred to x^1

Contradiction: WARP is violated; no rational preference generates this data.
slides.title: Worked example: testing WARP on data

slides.html:
3. Choice under Uncertainty

From bundles to lotteries
slides.title: 3. Choice under Uncertainty

slides.html:
Expected Utility Theorem

  • Axioms: complete, transitive, continuous, monotone, substitution/reduction ⟹ independence
  • ⟹ vNM utility U(g)=\sum_ip_iU(a_i), unique up to positive affine transformations
  • Construction: g\sim(U(g)\circ a_1,\,(1-U(g))\circ a_n) — the standard-lottery probability is the utility
slides.title: Expected Utility Theorem

slides.html:
Worked example: a vNM utility and the Allais paradox

U(0)=0, U(100)=1, a sure 50 \sim (100 w.p. 0.7) ⟹ U(50)=0.7.

g=(0.2\circ0,0.5\circ50,0.3\circ100): U(g)=0.35+0.3=0.65.

Allais: A\succB \iff 0.11U(1)>0.1U(5)+0.01U(0) \iff C\succD.

Choosing A and D contradicts independence: expected utility is an approximation, not a law.
slides.title: Worked example: a vNM utility and the Allais paradox

slides.html:
Worked example: risk premium and insurance

U=\sqrt w, gamble 0 or 100: E=50, E[U]=5, CE=25, premium 25. Small risk (90 or 110): premium 0.25=\tfrac12\lambda\sigma^2 (\lambda=0.005, \sigma^2=100).

Insurance: wealth 100, loss 36 w.p. \tfrac12: CE=81<E=82. Fair full cover costs 18 ⟹ sure 82 >81: she buys; she would pay up to 19.
slides.title: Worked example: risk premium and insurance

slides.html:
Arrow–Pratt and Stochastic Dominance

\lambda(x)=-\frac{U''}{U'},\quad R(x)=-\frac{xU''}{U'}

More risk averse ⟺ U_1=\phi(U_2), \phi concave ⟺ \lambda_1\ge\lambda_2

Small risks: r\approx\tfrac12\lambda\sigma^2

  • FOSD: F(x)\le G(x) for all x
  • SOSD: \int_{-\infty}^x F\le\int_{-\infty}^xG
  • CARA: -e^{-aw}; CRRA: w^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)
slides.title: Arrow–Pratt and Stochastic Dominance

slides.html:
Worked example: dominance

F: 2 or 4; G: 1 or 4 (each \tfrac12) ⟹ F FOSD G.

H: sure 3; K: 2 or 4 ⟹ H SOSD K (same mean, less risk).

With U=\sqrt w: E_F=1.707>1.5=E_G; \sqrt3=1.732>1.707.
slides.title: Worked example: dominance

slides.html:
Subjective Probability: Anscombe–Aumann

  • Act h:\Omega\to\Delta X (states have no objective probability, prizes do)
  • Independence + Archimedean + state independence ⟺ U(h)=\sum_s\mu(s)\sum_xh_s(x)U(x)
  • Probabilities are identified from choices: 3 dollars on "rain" for 1 on "no rain" ⟹ weights 3 : 1
slides.title: Subjective Probability: Anscombe–Aumann

slides.html:
4. Producer Theory

Almost exactly parallel to the consumer
slides.title: 4. Producer Theory

slides.html:
The Dictionary

Consumer Producer
utility U output f
expenditure e (concave) cost C (concave)
Shephard's lemma Shephard's lemma
indirect utility V / Roy profit \pi (convex) / Hotelling
Slutsky negative semi-definite substitution matrix: NSD for cost minimisation, PSD for profit maximisation
slides.title: The Dictionary

slides.html:
Production Sets and Returns to Scale

  • Y: no free lunch, inaction, free disposal, irreversibility
  • CRS f(tx)=tf(x); IRS >; DRS <; Y convex ⟺ f concave
  • Additive + non-increasing returns ⟺ convex cone
  • Profit maximisation may have no solution under CRS/IRS (profit 0 or +\infty)
slides.title: Production Sets and Returns to Scale

slides.html:
Cost Minimisation and Profit Maximisation

C(w,y)=\min wx\ \text{s.t.}\ f(x)\ge y

FOC: w_i=\lambda f_i, \lambda=MC

Conditional demands x(w,y)=\partial C/\partial w

\pi(p,w)=\max pf(x)-wx

FOC: pf_i=w_i

Hotelling: \partial\pi/\partial p=y, -\partial\pi/\partial w_i=x_i

\pi is convex and degree-one homogeneous in (p,w)
slides.title: Cost Minimisation and Profit Maximisation

slides.html:
Worked example: cost and profit

Cost. f=\sqrt{x_1x_2}, w=(1,4), y=10: MRTS=x_2/x_1=\tfrac14 ⟹ x=(20,5), C=40=2\sqrt{w_1w_2}\,y; Shephard: \partial C/\partial w_1=20 ✓.

Profit. f=\sqrt x, p=4, w=1: x=4, y=2, \pi=4=p^2/(4w); Hotelling: \partial\pi/\partial p=2=y ✓.
slides.title: Worked example: cost and profit

slides.html:
Worked example: cost curves

VC=y^3-6y^2+14y, fixed cost 10.

  • AVC minimum at y=3: AVC=MC=5 ⟹ shut down below price 5
  • ATC minimum near y=3.43: ATC\approx MC\approx8.1 ⟹ exit below about 8.1
  • between 5 and 8.1: produce at a loss in the short run (fixed cost sunk)
slides.title: Worked example: cost curves

slides.html:
5. General Equilibrium

Prices are the numbers that clear all markets at once
slides.title: 5. General Equilibrium

slides.html:
Excess Demand and Walras's Law

  • z(p)=\sum_ix^i(p,pe^i)-\sum_ie^i: continuous, degree-0 homogeneous
  • Walras's law: p\cdot z(p)=0 (sum the budget constraints)
  • n-1 markets clear ⟹ the n-th clears
  • Boundary: a price tending to 0 ⟹ unbounded excess demand for it
slides.title: Excess Demand and Walras's Law
Worked example: Alice and Bob trade

slides.html:
Existence (Brouwer)

Auctioneer map on the compact convex set S_\epsilon:

f_k(p)=\frac{\epsilon+p_k+\max\{0,\bar z_k\}}{n\epsilon+1+\sum_m\max\{0,\bar z_m\}}

  1. Brouwer ⟹ fixed point p^\epsilon
  2. \epsilon\to0: boundary property ⟹ p^*\gg0
  3. Walras's law ⟹ z(p^*)=0

With production: need y+\sum e\gg0
slides.title: Existence (Brouwer)

slides.html:
Worked example: Robinson Crusoe

3 hours, U=\sqrt{c\ell}, firm f(n)=\sqrt n, p=1.

Firm: n=\tfrac1{4w^2}, y=\tfrac1{2w}, \pi=\tfrac1{4w}. Labour market clears at w=\tfrac12.

n=1, y=c=1, \ell=2, \pi=\tfrac12; wage =f'(1)=\tfrac12 ✓.
slides.title: Worked example: Robinson Crusoe

slides.html:
6. The Welfare Theorems

Are markets efficient? Can efficiency and equity be separated?
slides.title: 6. The Welfare Theorems

slides.html:
First Welfare Theorem

Local non-satiation ⟹ every Walrasian equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient.

  • Proof: a better allocation is either unaffordable or affordable-but-unchosen ⟹ contradicts optimality in the budget
  • No convexity needed, and no claim about fairness
  • Core & equilibria: equilibria are in the core; Edgeworth–Debreu–Scarf: in replica economies the core shrinks to equilibria
slides.title: First Welfare Theorem

slides.html:
Worked example: is the equilibrium efficient?

MRS=x_2/x_1 at start at equilibrium
Alice 2/8=0.25 1
Bob 8/2=4 1

Different MRS at the start ⟹ trade helps both. Equal MRS (= price ratio) at the equilibrium ⟹ no further gains: Pareto efficient. Contract curve: the diagonal.
slides.title: Worked example: is the equilibrium efficient?

slides.html:
Second Welfare Theorem

Convexity + non-satiation ⟹ every Pareto-efficient allocation is supported by wealth transfers + competitive markets.

  1. Aggregate: V=\sum V_i and Y+\{e\} are convex
  2. Separate: efficiency ⟹ disjoint ⟹ separating hyperplane p
  3. Decentralise: p supports every consumer and firm
  • Social planner: weights \lambda maximise weighted utility; multiplier = price
slides.title: Second Welfare Theorem

slides.html:
Worked example: redistribute, then let markets work

Target: x^A=(7,7), x^B=(3,3) (efficient; MRS=1 ⟹ p=(1,1)).

  • wealth needed: Alice 14, Bob 6; endowments worth 10 each
  • lump-sum transfer: Bob → Alice, 4
  • each then chooses exactly the target bundle
slides.title: Worked example: redistribute, then let markets work

slides.html:
Failures and Extensions

  • Public goods: Lindahl personalised prices, \sum_iMRS_i=MRT (Samuelson); but nobody wants to reveal preferences
  • Non-convex technology: second theorem can fail; marginal-cost pricing needs subsidies
  • Time and uncertainty: state-contingent commodities; Arrow–Debreu ⟺ Radner (complete securities)
slides.title: Failures and Extensions

slides.html:
Worked example: a public good

MC=8; MB_A=10-q, MB_B=6-q.

  • efficient (Samuelson): MB_A+MB_B=8 ⟹ q=4
  • private: Alice stops at q=2; Bob free-rides ⟹ underprovision
  • Lindahl: r_A=6, r_B=2 (=8) ⟹ both demand 4

Needs each person's true MB; they will understate it. Chapter 11.
slides.title: Worked example: a public good

slides.html:
7. Static Games

I must predict you; you must predict me
slides.title: 7. Static Games

slides.html:
Strategic Form and the Prisoner's Dilemma

Cooperate Defect
Cooperate 3, 3 0, 4
Defect 4, 0 1, 1
  • Defect is strictly dominant ⟹ unique NE (Defect, Defect) =(1,1)
  • Deleting strictly dominated strategies is order-independent; deleting weakly dominated ones is not reliable
slides.title: Strategic Form and the Prisoner's Dilemma

slides.html:
Worked example: iterated deletion

L M R
T 1, 0 1, 2 0, 1
B 0, 3 0, 1 2, 0

R is dominated by M ⟹ delete; then B is dominated by T ⟹ delete; then Column picks M.

Unique survivor (T,M) = Nash equilibrium, found without guessing.
slides.title: Worked example: iterated deletion

slides.html:
Worked example: battle of the sexes

O F
O 2, 1 0, 0
F 0, 0 1, 2

Pure: (O,O), (F,F). Mixed: Row plays O w.p. p=\tfrac23 (makes Column indifferent), Column q=\tfrac13 (makes Row indifferent). Payoff \tfrac23 each: worse than either pure equilibrium.
slides.title: Worked example: battle of the sexes

slides.html:
Existence and Correlated Equilibrium

  • Nash: finite games have a mixed equilibrium (best-response correspondence satisfies Kakutani)
  • Rationalizability: iteratively delete never-best-response strategies
  • Correlated equilibrium: obeying the recommendation is optimal; the set is convex and contains Nash
slides.title: Existence and Correlated Equilibrium

slides.html:
8. Dynamic Games

Non-credible threats
slides.title: 8. Dynamic Games

slides.html:
Worked example: entry deterrence in numbers

Payoffs (entrant, incumbent): stay out (0,4); enter–accommodate (2,2); enter–fight (-1,-1).

  • incumbent: 2>-1 ⟹ accommodate
  • entrant: 2>0 ⟹ enter
  • (Stay out, Fight) is Nash but the threat is not credible
slides.title: Worked example: entry deterrence in numbers

slides.html:
One-Shot Deviation Principle

Finite perfect-information game: s^* is an SPE ⟺ no profitable one-shot deviation.

  • Infinite horizon: needs continuity at infinity
  • Check every history, on or off the path
slides.title: One-Shot Deviation Principle

slides.html:
Worked example: splitting a pie

\delta_1,\delta_2 First proposer gets
0.9,\ 0.9 0.1/0.19=0.526
0.9,\ 0.6 0.4/0.46=0.870
0.5,\ 0.5 2/3
\to1 \to\tfrac12

Responder is indifferent: 0.9\times0.526=0.474.
slides.title: Worked example: splitting a pie

slides.html:
Repeated Games and the Folk Theorem

  • Trigger strategy: cooperation sustainable ⟺ \delta\ge\dfrac{4-3}{4-1}=\dfrac13
  • F^*=F\cap\{v_i\ge\underline v_i\} (feasible, individually rational)
  • Folk: if F^* has interior, every v\in F^* is an SPE payoff for large \delta

Almost too many equilibria: patience buys a huge set, predictive power drops.
slides.title: Repeated Games and the Folk Theorem

slides.html:
Worked example: when does cooperation survive?

Prisoner's dilemma (3 / 4 / 1), trigger strategy:

  • cooperate for ever: \dfrac3{1-\delta}; cheat once: 4+\dfrac\delta{1-\delta}
  • equilibrium iff \delta\ge\tfrac13
  • \delta=0.9: 30 vs 13

Cooperation needs patience.
slides.title: Worked example: when does cooperation survive?

slides.html:
9. Games of Incomplete Information

Model "not knowing" as types
slides.title: 9. Games of Incomplete Information

slides.html:
Bayesian Games and PBE

  • BNE: each type best-responds in conditional expectation
  • PBE = sequential rationality + Bayes' rule (off-path beliefs free)
  • Sequential equilibrium: beliefs are limits of completely mixed strategies ⟹ PBE; SE ⟹ SPE
slides.title: Bayesian Games and PBE

slides.html:
Worked example: a Bayesian Cournot game

P=12-q_1-q_2; firm 2's cost 0 or 4 (equally likely, private).

q_2^L=\tfrac{12-q_1}2, q_2^H=\tfrac{8-q_1}2, q_1=\tfrac{12-E[q_2]}2

⟹ q_1=\tfrac{14}3, q_2^L=\tfrac{11}3, q_2^H=\tfrac53.

Firm 2's strategy is a function of its type.
slides.title: Worked example: a Bayesian Cournot game

slides.html:
Signalling Games

Nature draws type → sender signals → receiver acts

  • Separating: signal reveals the type
  • Pooling: types send the same signal

Intuitive criterion: if a type can never gain from an off-path signal m whatever the receiver's best response, beliefs should give it zero weight.
slides.title: Signalling Games

slides.html:
Worked example: Bayes' rule on a signal

Prior "strong" =0.3; strong always signals, weak signals w.p. 0.5:

\mu=\frac{0.3}{0.3+0.7\cdot0.5}\approx0.46

Pooling: belief unchanged. Separating: belief \to1.
slides.title: Worked example: Bayes' rule on a signal

slides.html:
Worked example: education as a signal

Productivity 2 or 1; education costs e (high), 2e (low).

  • separating: low does not mimic iff e^*\ge0.5; high agrees iff e^*\le1
  • intuitive criterion picks e^*=0.5: payoffs 1.5 and 1
  • pooling (wage 1.5) fails: e=0.4 is attractive only to the high type
slides.title: Worked example: education as a signal

slides.html:
10. Information Economics

Hidden information and hidden action
slides.title: 10. Information Economics

slides.html:
Adverse Selection: Insurance

  • Full information: B=L, p=\pi_iL, full insurance
  • Asymmetric: p^*=E[\pi\mid\pi\ge h(p^*)]L ⟹ death spiral, low-risk types priced out
  • Akerlof's lemons in insurance form
slides.title: Adverse Selection: Insurance

slides.html:
Worked example: the death spiral

U=\sqrt w, wealth 100, loss 100; \pi_L=0.1, \pi_H=0.5.

  1. full information: low pays 10, 9.49>9: buys
  2. one price: fair price 30 ⟹ low gets \sqrt{70}=8.37<9: leaves
  3. only high remain ⟹ price 50 ⟹ high still buys (7.07>5)
slides.title: Worked example: the death spiral

slides.html:
Principal–Agent: Hidden Type

  • Two types: efficient S'(\underline q)=\underline\theta (no distortion at the top)
  • Inefficient: S'(\bar q)=\bar\theta+\dfrac v{1-v}(\bar\theta-\underline\theta) (output distorted down)
  • Continuum: S'(q)=\theta+\dfrac{F(\theta)}{f(\theta)} (virtual cost); rent U(\theta)=\int_\theta^{\bar\theta}q

Trade efficiency for rent: depress the inefficient type's output to cut the rent paid to the efficient type.
slides.title: Principal–Agent: Hidden Type

slides.html:
Worked example: the contract menu

S=2\sqrt q, \theta\in\{1,2\}, prob. \tfrac12 each.

Efficient \underline\theta=1 Inefficient \bar\theta=2
full information q 1 \tfrac14
hidden type q 1 (no distortion) \tfrac19
wage \tfrac{10}9 (incl. rent \tfrac19) \tfrac29

Profit 0.75\to0.667: the cost of not knowing the type.
slides.title: Worked example: the contract menu

slides.html:
Moral Hazard

  • MLRP: larger loss ⟹ looks more like no effort
  • Full information: Borch condition ⟹ full insurance
  • To induce effort: \dfrac1{u'}=\lambda+\Big(1-\dfrac{\pi_l(0)}{\pi_l(1)}\Big)\mu, \mu>0 ⟹ the agent must bear risk
  • Trade-off: risk sharing vs incentives
slides.title: Moral Hazard

slides.html:
Worked example: the cost of the incentive

u=\sqrt w; effort costs 1; success prob. 0.8 (work) vs 0.4 (shirk); reservation utility 3.

  • incentive: \sqrt{w_1}-\sqrt{w_0}\ge2.5; participation ⟹ w_0=4, w_1=20.25
  • expected wage 17; with observable effort a sure 16 suffices

Incentive cost =1: the agent must bear risk and be paid for it.
slides.title: Worked example: the cost of the incentive

slides.html:
11. Mechanism Design

How to make the rules
slides.title: 11. Mechanism Design

slides.html:
Worked example: auctions in numbers

Values (70,50,30), second price: winner pays 50, earns 20; any other bid never helps.

Two bidders, uniform values, first price: b=v/2. v=0.8: bid 0.4 earns 0.32; bid 0.5 earns only 0.30.

Revenue: second price =E[\text{lower value}]=\tfrac13; first price =\tfrac12E[\text{higher}]=\tfrac13. Equal.
slides.title: Worked example: auctions in numbers

slides.html:
Revelation Principle and IC

Every BNE of any mechanism has an equivalent truthful direct mechanism.

A direct mechanism is incentive compatible ⟺

  1. \bar P_i(\cdot) non-decreasing
  2. \bar C_i(v)=\bar C_i(0)+\bar P_i(v)v-\int_0^v\bar P_i(x)dx

Revenue equivalence: same \bar P and \bar C(0) ⟹ same expected revenue
slides.title: Revelation Principle and IC

slides.html:
Myerson's Optimal Auction

E[R]=E\Big[\sum_iP_i(v)\,\psi_i(v_i)\Big],\qquad\psi_i(v_i)=v_i-\frac{1-F_i(v_i)}{f_i(v_i)}
  • Give the good to the bidder with the highest, positive virtual valuation; otherwise keep it
  • Uniform: \psi=2v-1 ⟹ second-price auction with reserve \frac12
  • Optimal ≠ efficient: the seller creates inefficiency to extract rent
slides.title: Myerson's Optimal Auction

slides.html:
Worked example: the optimal reserve

Two uniform bidders, \psi=2v-1, reserve \tfrac12:

Event Prob. Revenue
both below \tfrac12 \tfrac14 0
exactly one above \tfrac12 \tfrac12
both above \tfrac14 \tfrac23

Revenue =\tfrac5{12}\approx0.417>\tfrac13, but unsold w.p. \tfrac14 even though both buyers value the good.

slides.html:
Ideas to Take Away

  • Optimisation + duality + envelope theorem generate all the "lemmas"
  • Convexity is the key to the welfare theorems; non-convexity, externalities and public goods cause failure
  • Credibility: threats must be optimal at every history
  • Asymmetric information creates rents, distortion and market failure
  • Truth-telling can be designed

References: Mas-Colell–Whinston–Green; Jehle–Reny; Fudenberg–Tirole; Laffont–Martimort; Krishna.
